title: Is Private Credit the Next Systemic Crisis? Steve Liesman Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 53

metadata.title: Is Private Credit the Next Systemic Crisis? Steve Liesman Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 53

summary: Recorded March 31, Steve Liesman and Eisman discuss overlapping oil, tariff, monetary-policy and private-credit risks. Eisman emphasizes U.S. resilience and bank capital while expecting software losses. Liesman challenges simple tariff-forecast grading and introduces hidden layers of leverage. A key qualification is that most private loans already carry floating rates, weakening a blanket refinancing-rate-cliff explanation. Bank of America data support lower-income stress alongside continued aggregate spending growth.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman hosts Steve Liesman. Liesman provides Fed reporting and several explicitly exploratory risks; Eisman supplies his own software, bank-resilience and policy interpretations.
framework_points: Evaluate conditional forecasts against the policy actually implemented.
Separate gross spending transfers from aggregate GDP losses.
Distinguish supply constraints from demand and inflation-expectation channels.
Trace leverage through fund, borrower and investor layers.
Software survival can coexist with impaired pricing and valuation.
Use private transaction data alongside representative official statistics.
tools_and_charts: Floating-rate resets, interest coverage and maturities.
Income-stratified Bank of America spending data.
transcript_cautions: Full transcript read in two contiguous parts including multiple advertisement breaks and closing recap.
Explicit recording date March 31, earlier than April 6 publication.
Steve Liesman and Steve Eisman are distinct speakers; the guest reports some third-party views without endorsing them.
Debt/equity and asset/equity leverage ratios are used loosely in dialogue and should not be compared without normalization.

evidence.title: Private Credit Growth and Monetary Policy Transmission
evidence.finding: Direct-lending and leveraged loans usually float off SOFR and reset every one to three months. Higher policy rates therefore already affect interest expense before maturity; refinancing can still alter spreads, covenants and principal availability.

evidence.title: H.8 bank balance sheets December 18 2009
evidence.finding: Historical H.8 tables record trillions in bank loans, including large commercial, real-estate and consumer portfolios; these are comparable categories for testing claims of zero subsequent bank loan growth. PDF text inspected; screenshot retrieval failed.

evidence.title: H.8 bank balance sheets November 6 2026
evidence.finding: All-commercial-bank loans and leases exceed $14 trillion, with commercial and industrial loans near $3 trillion and real-estate loans about $5.9 trillion. Banks have contributed substantial post-crisis credit growth, though categories and reporting conventions require adjustments for exact growth shares.

claims.next_check: Compare consistent bank and nonbank lending series. The literal claim is suspect; the inspected H.8 correction is documented separately in the Hirsch episode.
